## Problem 1

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)
```

```{r load_noaa}
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r }
## A noaa sumnary
n_rows = nrow(ny_noaa)
n_cols = ncol(ny_noaa)
n_stations = n_distinct(pull(ny_noaa, id))
first_date = min(pull(ny_noaa, date))
last_date = max(pull(ny_noaa, date))
pct_missing_prcp = round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, prcp))) * 100, 1)
pct_missing_snow = round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, snow))) * 100, 1)
pct_missing_tmax = round(mean(is.na(pull(ny_noaa, tmax))) * 100, 1)
```

The dataset contains daily weather records from 747 weather stations in New York, from 1981-01-01 to 2010-12-31. It has 2595176 rows and 7 columns. Missing data is a major issue, especially for maximum temperature, 43.7% of values are missing, compared with 14.7% of snowfall and 5.6% of precipitation values.

```{r}
## Data cleaning
ny_noaa |> drop_na(tmax) |> pull(tmax) |> head()

noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |> separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    month = as.numeric(month),
    day = as.numeric(day),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10)
```

### For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?

```{r snow_common}
noaa_df |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

The most common snowfall value is 0, because it does not snow on most days 
of the year. 


### Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers?

```{r warning = FALSE}
noaa_df |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |>
  mutate(month = case_match(month, 1 ~ "January", 7 ~ "July")) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3, size = .5) +
  geom_line(alpha = .3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average max temperature by station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average max temperature in °C"
  )
```

Average max temperatures in July is around 25–30°C and are much higher than in 
January (-5 to 5°C), and January varies more from year to year. 
There are a few outliers, such as individual stations with a super
cold July or January compared with others in the same year.


### Make a two-panel plot showing (i) tmax vs tmin for the full dataset (note that a scatterplot may not be the best option); and (ii) make a plot showing the distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100 separately by year.

```{r warning = FALSE, fig.asp = 1}
tmax_tmin_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex() +
  labs(
    title = "Max vs. min temperature",
    x = "Min temp (°C)",
    y = "Max temp (°C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

snow_plot =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(scale = .85) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall by year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
  )

tmax_tmin_plot + snow_plot
```

Max and min temperature have a strong positive relationship. And the snowfall distributions are very similar across years.


## Problem 2

### Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets

```{r warning = FALSE}
covar_df =
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, na = c("NA", "", ".")) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(sex, 1 ~ "male", 2 ~ "female"),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")))

accel_df =
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims") |>
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

nhanes_df =
  inner_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")
```

### Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category,

```{r edu_sex_table}
covar_df |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category.

```{r age_dist_plot}
covar_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Age distribution by education and sex",
    x = "Education",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex")
```

According to the table, more than high school category has the most participants. In the high school equivalent category, men outnumber women, others have more women. Participants with less than high school education tend to be older, and those with more than high school education tend to be younger. Women in the high school equivalent group are older on average than men in that group.


### Using your tidied dataset, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant.

```{r total_activity, message = FALSE}
total_activity_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims))
```
